```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2, fig.align = "center",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svglite" else "png",
  fig.ext = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svg" else "png",
  dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
library(metrodag)
```

## Start with the space the figure must occupy

The same DAG may need to fit a manuscript column, a slide, or a supplementary
page. Decide the intended width, output format, and font early. Metrodag places
labels when the figure is drawn, so a clear RStudio preview is not a substitute
for checking the exported file.

This guide is self-contained and continues the illustrative smoking example
from [Getting started](metrodag.html). See the [analysis guide](analysis-views.html)
for the meaning of its role markers and adjustment annotations.

```{r graph}
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("C", "C", "X", "X", "M"),
  to   = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y")
)
display_labels <- c(C = "Socioeconomic background", X = "Cigarettes per day",
  M = "Tar deposits", Y = "Lung cancer")
p <- metro_dag(edges, labels = display_labels,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C")
fixed <- attr(p, "metrodag_layout")
```

## Choose a visual style

The default `style = "publication"` uses restrained lines on white. Monochrome
retains distinctions through shapes, fills, and dashes. Metro style colours
visual paths through the drawing; those colours do not encode effect magnitude,
statistical significance, or valid adjustment sets.

```{r monochrome, fig.cap="Monochrome preserves the exposure, outcome, and adjustment markers.", fig.alt="The four-node smoking DAG in black and white, with C shown as an adjusted square and X and Y shown as filled markers."}
mono <- metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels,
  style = "monochrome", family = "sans")
mono
```

```{r metro-style, fig.cap="Metro colours describe visual paths rather than causal quantities.", fig.alt="The identical graph in metro style, with coloured routes and unchanged causal arrows and role markers."}
metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels, style = "metro")
```

Use `family` to choose a font installed on the machine that will render the
figure. Generic `"sans"` and `"serif"` are portable choices, but their actual
fonts can differ between systems. Check the saved PDF or SVG with your intended
font, particularly when another computer will display it.

### Adjust a style

The named styles are presets of `metro_style()`. Start from one and change only
what the journal or the figure needs: role colours, the arrowhead, the width of
the background casing at crossings, how stations grow with their degree, the
legend wording and its position. A style object is passed to `style`:

```{r custom-style, fig.cap="A custom style keeps the geometry and changes only colours, arrowheads and legend text.", fig.alt="The smoking DAG with green exposure and purple outcome markers, a legend on the right that reads Treatment and Response, and uniform station sizes."}
journal <- metro_style(
  exposure_fill = "#1B9E77", outcome_fill = "#7570B3",
  legend_labels = c(exposure = "Treatment", outcome = "Response"),
  legend_position = "right", station_scaling = "none", arrow_length = 1.6
)
metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels, style = journal)
```

By default, stations with many arrows grow a little so their arrow tips stay
distinct (`station_scaling = "capped"`, at most 1.5 times `node_size`). Use
`"none"` for uniform stations or `"degree"` for the unbounded growth of earlier
versions. `casing_width = 0` removes the background gap painted under each
route at crossings; keep it when arrows cross.

### Style individual arrows

`edge_style` changes the linetype, colour or width of named arrows without
touching the layout, roles or any check. Dotted arrows are a common way to mark
relationships that are assumed but uncertain:

```{r edge-style, fig.cap="Per-arrow styles mark an uncertain relationship and emphasise the pathway of interest.", fig.alt="The smoking DAG with a dotted arrow from socioeconomic background to lung cancer and a thicker arrow from cigarettes per day to tar deposits."}
metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels,
  edge_style = list("C->Y" = list(linetype = "dotted"),
    "X->M" = list(width = 0.8)))
```

Add `edge_legend = c(dotted = "Assumed, uncertain")` to explain a linetype in
the legend, or describe the convention in the figure caption.

### Distinguish roles without colour

In greyscale print, exposure and outcome should differ by shape as well as
colour. `metro_style(outcome_marker = "ring")` draws the outcome as a hollow
ring with a filled centre; the monochrome preset uses it by default.

## Make labels readable

Labels wrap automatically. The `label_wrap` argument is an approximate character
limit, and physical space on the device also affects wrapping. Keep identifiers
short and use the `labels` vector for the full text.

When you need an intentional break, use `\n`. Explicit breaks are retained;
`label_wrap = NULL` disables additional automatic wrapping:

```{r manual-labels, fig.cap="Manual line breaks provide consistent wording across a small figure.", fig.alt="The graph uses two-line labels for socioeconomic background, cigarettes per day, and tar deposits."}
short_labels <- c(C = "Socioeconomic\nbackground", X = "Cigarettes\nper day",
  M = "Tar\ndeposits", Y = "Lung cancer")
compact <- metro_dag(fixed, labels = short_labels, label_wrap = NULL,
  style = "monochrome")
compact
```

Use labels that a reader can understand without consulting the R code. If one
label still needs a small adjustment after choosing the final size, use a named
nudge. Positive values move right and up, in millimetres:

```{r nudge}
nudged <- metro_dag(fixed, labels = short_labels, label_wrap = NULL,
  style = "monochrome", label_nudge = list(C = c(0, 2)))
nudge_report <- diagnose_metro_dag(nudged, width = 180, device = "svg")
nudge_report$issues
```

A nudge moves only the label. It may introduce a new conflict, so diagnose and
inspect the result. The original `compact` plot remains available. Avoid using
many nudges to compensate for a figure that is simply too small.

## Add a title or caption

Standard ggplot annotations work. Metrodag wraps them using the output device's
font metrics:

```{r title, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Titles and captions are part of the figure's available physical space.", fig.alt="The smoking DAG with a title describing the assumed pathways and a caption identifying it as a teaching example."}
captioned <- mono + ggplot2::labs(
  title = "Assumed pathways from cigarettes per day to lung cancer",
  caption = "Illustrative teaching model; arrows represent assumed relationships."
)
captioned
```

Leave enough height for titles, the legend, and any adjustment subtitle. If a
journal puts captions outside the image, supply the explanatory text in the
manuscript instead. Keep a legend when the role markers would otherwise be
ambiguous.

## Change orientation or impose temporal structure

Choose `direction = "right"` (the default), `"left"`, `"down"`, or `"up"`
when constructing the layout. To change orientation, rebuild from
the graph rather than passing `direction` alongside an existing layout:

```{r orientation, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="A downward layout can suit a taller page region.", fig.alt="The same four-variable graph laid out with causal arrows progressing downward."}
metro_dag(edges, direction = "down", labels = short_labels, label_wrap = NULL,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C")
```

For longitudinal graphs, explicit `rank` values can represent survey waves.
Ranks must strictly increase along every arrow. Their order and ties matter;
the numerical gaps do not set physical distances. Nodes linked by a same-wave
arrow need different ranks, even if both were measured in the same survey wave.

The following example assumes arrows between successive waves and a background
factor `C` measured before wave 1:

```{r longitudinal-input}
wave_edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("C", "C", "X1", "X2", "Y1", "Y2", "X1", "Y1", "X2", "Y2"),
  to   = c("X1", "Y1", "X2", "X3", "Y2", "Y3", "Y2", "X2", "Y3", "X3")
)
wave_labels <- c(C = "Background",
  X1 = "Smoking: wave 1", X2 = "Smoking: wave 2", X3 = "Smoking: wave 3",
  Y1 = "Lung function: wave 1", Y2 = "Lung function: wave 2", Y3 = "Lung function: wave 3")
wave_ranks <- c(C = 0, X1 = 1, Y1 = 1, X2 = 2, Y2 = 2, X3 = 3, Y3 = 3)
```

`align` explicitly names repeated variables that should occupy one row in a
horizontal drawing, or one column in a vertical drawing. The package does not
infer repeated-measure identity from similar node names.

```{r longitudinal, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Explicit ranks order the waves; alignment keeps repeated variables on consistent rows.", fig.alt="A background variable precedes two aligned three-wave chains: smoking and lung function. Cross-lagged arrows join the chains between waves."}
longitudinal <- metro_dag(wave_edges,
  labels = wave_labels, rank = wave_ranks,
  align = list(c("X1", "X2", "X3"), c("Y1", "Y2", "Y3")),
  exposure = "X1", outcome = "Y3", adjusted = "C")
longitudinal
```

`rank_labels` names each rank, for example the survey waves, above a
horizontal drawing or beside a vertical one:

```{r rank-labels, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Rank headers name the survey waves.", fig.alt="The longitudinal DAG with bold headers Baseline, Wave 1, Wave 2 and Wave 3 above its ranks."}
metro_dag(wave_edges, labels = wave_labels, rank = wave_ranks,
  align = list(c("X1", "X2", "X3"), c("Y1", "Y2", "Y3")),
  exposure = "X1", outcome = "Y3", adjusted = "C",
  rank_labels = c("Baseline", "Wave 1", "Wave 2", "Wave 3"))
```

Alignment is a readability choice and can increase crossings, bends, or space.
To assess that trade-off, compare with the same graph and ranks but without
`align`. Avoid deleting substantively necessary arrows just to simplify a
drawing. The larger longitudinal DAG in the
[six-example gallery](https://github.com/hdbt/metrodag/blob/main/inst/benchmarks/REPORT.md)
includes both aligned and rank-only exports.

## Export at the intended dimensions

The widths below are examples; follow the target journal's requirements.
`save_metro_dag()` defaults to millimetres, with `units = "cm"` or `"in"`
also available.

| Output | Example | Why use it? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| PDF | `save_metro_dag("dag.pdf", p, width = "double")` | Vector output for manuscripts |
| EPS | `save_metro_dag("dag.eps", p, width = "single")` | Vector output for journals that still require PostScript |
| SVG | `save_metro_dag("dag.svg", p, width = 180)` | Vector output for the web or an editor |
| PNG | `save_metro_dag("dag.png", p, width = 180, dpi = 600)` | Raster output when requested |
| TIFF | `save_metro_dag("dag.tiff", p, width = 180, dpi = 600)` | LZW-compressed raster submission format |

The width presets `"single"` (85 mm), `"1.5"` (120 mm) and `"double"`
(180 mm) stand for common journal column widths; a number in `units` works
just as well. PDF and EPS use Cairo devices, which embed fonts; if Cairo is
unavailable, a warning reports the fallback to the base devices.

When omitted, height is calculated automatically, within 45–220 mm. Supply
`height` when the figure needs a different size. Text and station sizes are
physical dimensions, so reducing width does not simply shrink every element.
Increasing raster `dpi` improves pixel resolution but does not create more
physical space for labels.

This example checks a candidate 85 mm single-column figure before saving it.
The temporary directory keeps the executed examples separate from your files.

```{r final-check}
final_report <- diagnose_metro_dag(compact, width = 85, device = "pdf")
final_report
final_report$issues
```

```{r export}
figure_dir <- tempdir()
save_metro_dag("smoking-column.pdf", compact,
  path = figure_dir, width = 85)
save_metro_dag("smoking-wide.svg", captioned,
  path = figure_dir, width = 180)
save_metro_dag("smoking-wide.png", captioned,
  path = figure_dir, width = 180, dpi = 300)
```

The directory supplied as `path` must already exist. If rendering fails, an
existing destination file is preserved. `ggplot2::ggsave()` also supports these
plots, but `save_metro_dag()` additionally provides automatic height and the
publication-oriented export defaults used here.

## Combine figures

MetroDAG plots are ggplots, so patchwork and `ggplot2::ggplotGrob()` work and
labels keep the plot's own margins. Titles are wrapped to the final width only
when the figure is drawn through MetroDAG, so wrap a titled figure with
`as_metro_grob()` before composing it. Side by side at 180 mm, the titled
figure would be too narrow to keep its arrows clear of the stations, so the
two figures are stacked, and the composition is checked at its final size
before it is saved:

```{r combine, eval = requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)}
library(patchwork)
combined <- wrap_elements(full = as_metro_grob(captioned)) / compact
combined_report <- diagnose_metro_dag(combined, width = 180, height = 180)
combined_report$ok
if (combined_report$ok) save_metro_dag("combined.pdf", combined,
  path = figure_dir, width = 180, height = 180)
```

`save_metro_dag()` and `diagnose_metro_dag()` check every MetroDAG panel of a
composition as strictly as a single figure; give them the composition's
height, since automatic height applies only to single figures and comparisons.

While drafting in a small preview pane, `on_error = "warn"` draws what fits and
reports the problems once instead of stopping. `save_metro_dag()` still refuses
to write such a figure unless it is also given `on_error = "warn"`.

## Diagnose problems systematically

`diagnose_metro_dag()` renders privately using the requested output format. Its
`issues` table identifies affected nodes or arrows and, for comparisons, panel
numbers. Use the same width, height, font, and format as the final export.

| Symptom | First response |
|:--|:--|
| Labels overlap | Increase the width, use concise labels, or allow automatic wrapping |
| One label touches an arrow | Inspect a small `label_nudge` at the final size |
| Arrow or station clearance fails | Give the complete graph more physical space |
| A long comparison title squeezes a panel | Use `ncol = 1`, shorten the title, or increase dimensions |
| A temporal rank is rejected | Check that every arrow goes to a strictly higher rank |
| A custom layout has a collapsed or incomplete route | Recompute the layout from the graph |
| The figure differs from the preview | Check the export device, dimensions, and installed font |

Warnings do not set `report$ok` to `FALSE`; read `report$issues` even when the
overall status passes. An empty issues table means no implemented conflict was
detected, not that the figure is optimal. Inspect arrowheads, dashed routes,
label-to-node associations, and the legend in the actual file.

Use `layout_metrics()` for geometric comparisons such as crossings and bends.
Those metrics complement device diagnostics: they do not measure readability
of the final text or correctness of the causal assumptions.

```{r metrics}
layout_metrics(attr(longitudinal, "metrodag_layout"))
```

## Keep the figure reproducible

Save the edge table or source graph, labels, role arguments, explicit constraints,
and export call in your analysis script. Record `packageVersion("metrodag")`
and `sessionInfo()` with the project. Layouts are deterministic for a given
input and package implementation, but algorithm updates can change geometry;
font and device differences can also change label placement.

For more complex examples, inspect the
[six annotated DAGs](https://github.com/hdbt/metrodag/blob/main/inst/benchmarks/REPORT.md)
and their [complete generation script](https://github.com/hdbt/metrodag/blob/main/data-raw/annotated_gallery.R).
For the layout search and its limitations, read
[Algorithm and constraints](algorithm.html).
